title: RSI under 30 on SPY won 76% of 146 trades since 2000 and still finished behind just holding it
author: person-person12
selftext:
Every free course teaches the same entry. RSI 14 closes under 30, thats oversold, buy it, and sell when it closes back over 50. I ran exactly that in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) on SPY daily candles from January 2000 to the end of March 2026, 6,599 candles, with commission and slippage charged on both sides of every fill.

146 trades. **76% of them won.** Profit factor 2.15, net +252.9% on a $10,000 account.

Then I ran "buy SPY and hold it" over the exact same candles with the same cost model. **+343.1%.**

So the rule wins three out of every four trades and finishes about 90 points of return behind doing nothing at all. The reason is sitting in the trade list, the average winner is about **two thirds the size** of the average loser. It takes small wins quickly and sits in the bad ones, because the only exit is RSI back over 50, and RSI does not come back over 50 while the market is actually falling.

February 2020 is the clearest one. It bought the oversold reading on the 25th and the exit condition did not trigger until March 27th, one trade, **negative $6,495.** Thats what a rule with no stop in it does, and no stop is exactly how its taught.

Fair warning on one number, the run ends with a position still open, so the last trade is marked at the close on March 30th and it was down $2,084 right then.

The one place the rule genuinely wins is the drawdown. **31.4% against 56.5%** for holding, because it is out of the market most of the time.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the rule sits in cash for most of those 26 years, so losing to buy and hold is mostly a time in market gap, not a bad entry. the fairer comparison is return per day actually exposed, or the same run with the idle cash parked in T-bills. it probably still loses, just by a lot less than the headline. the forward half is what I made Quantradin for, the same rule running on live prices with fake money. quantradin.com.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea thats fair, the time in market gap is doing a lot of the work there. **Return per day actually exposed** is the right comparison and I didnt run it that way. Parking the idle cash in T-bills I can add too. Did yours still finish behind once the cash was earning?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: honestly I never ran the version with the cash earning, so I can't tell you. my guess is the gap shrinks a lot, since most of what buy and hold had over the rule was just more days in the market.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Youre right, and thats the version I should have run. 146 trades across 26 years is barely any time in the market, so **the idle cash is doing most of the work in that comparison**. Ill run it again with a yield on the flat days and post what it comes back with.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the T-bill version is the one I'd trust. use the actual 3-month yield day by day rather than a flat rate though, 2009 to 2015 was near zero and that changes the picture more than people expect.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Youre right and a flat rate across 2000 to 2026 is doing a lot of quiet work. Near zero for six years then over 5%, averaged into one number, flatters the cash leg in exactly the stretch where SPY ran. If i do that version it has to be the daily yield.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, daily it is. the flat rate was me being lazy, and it happens to be lazy in exactly the direction that flatters the strategy.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea, a flat rate is harmless until the thing starts taking ten times the trades. Then **its the number that decides the result.** I ran the same breakout on 5, 15 and 60 minute candles this morning. The only reason the fast one lost was the bill.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: same signal, different bill per trade, opposite verdict. that's the fast timeframe in one line.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Thats it in one line yea. I ran one breakout on NQ, ES and gold tonight over the same five years and **all three were green before costs**. The bill flipped two of them into losers without a single rule changing.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: two of three flipping on costs alone is the result nobody posts. which one held up, gold?

comments.author: Corpulos
comments.body: Do you have an RSI lower limit exit? For example,  sell if RSI <25.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: No, the only exit was a close back over 50, so anything that kept falling just sat in the trade until it came back. A floor at 25 cuts those off but it also **books the loss at about the worst point** in a lot of them, which is where the 76% win rate would start coming apart. Did you have a re-entry sitting behind it, or is 25 a straight get out?

replies.author: Corpulos
replies.body:
Perhaps you could screen which ones to drop at RSI=25 based on some fundamental indicator such as PE or Altman Z score.

By the way, is this data set available in Colab?

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: On SPY theres nothing to screen, its a single index, so a PE or Z score filter would mean running the same thing name by name across a basket instead. And no Colab export, the candles and the full trade list sit in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=reply&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading).

replies.author: Corpulos
replies.body:
Yeah, my idea was to run it name by name. But as it turns out none of the SPY stocks had a negagive PE. 

Anyways, what is the idel money being held in? I mean, are you just holding cash until the RSI  for a stock is triggered. That wouldn't be fair.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Yea its flat in cash between trades and earns nothing, no interest credited on the idle balance.

Youre right that its not a clean comparison, but it cuts **against** the RSI side and not for it. Credit it a bill yield for the time its out of the market and it closes some of the gap. It still finished behind holding.
